extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners, patent attorneys, agents, and applicants (practitioners involved in prosecution/defense of patent claims)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on when and how a patent reference's broad disclosure (including nonpreferred or alternative embodiments) may be used to reject claimed subject matter, and how 'teaching away' should be treated in anticipation/obviousness rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents are relevant as prior art for all they contain
rubrics_metrics.description: "The use of patents as references is not limited to what the patentees describe as their own inventions or to the problems with which they are concerned. They are part of the literature of the art, relevant for all they contain." (In re Heck, quoting In re Lemelson.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents should be treated like technical literature: examiners may rely on any disclosure in a patent when determining prior art, not only the preferred embodiments or the patentee's stated focus. The page cites In re Heck (and In re Lemelson) as authority for this broad use of patents as references.

rubrics_metrics.name: A reference may be relied upon for all it would have reasonably suggested to one of ordinary skill
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference is usable for whatever it would have reasonably suggested to a person having ordinary skill in the art, including nonpreferred embodiments (Merck & Co. v. Biocraft Labs., Inc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When making a rejection, consider not only the explicit preferred embodiment but also other embodiments or suggestions a skilled artisan would reasonably take from the reference. Examples cited: Upsher-Smith (optional inclusion of a component teaches compositions both with and without that component) and Celeritas (a disclosure of a suboptimal option is still a disclosure and can anticipate claims). See also MPEP §§2131.05 and 2145 for discussion of prior art that 'teaches away' in anticipation and obviousness contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonpreferred and alternative embodiments constitute prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosed examples and preferred embodiments do not constitute a teaching away from a broader disclosure or nonpreferred embodiments (In re Susi). A known or obvious composition does not become patentable merely because it is described as somewhat inferior to another product (In re Gurley).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat a patent's discussion of preferred embodiments as limiting the scope of what the patent teaches for prior-art purposes. Statements that an embodiment is 'inferior' are insufficient, by themselves, to remove that embodiment from the prior art. The Gurley case indicates that asserting inferiority does not overcome a rejection unless there is a discovery beyond what was known in the art. Use these principles when evaluating anticipation or obviousness rejections based on a patent disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure of multiple alternatives does not, by itself, teach away from any of those alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: "The prior art's mere disclosure of more than one alternative does not constitute a teaching away from any of these alternatives because such disclosure does not criticize, discredit, or otherwise discourage the solution claimed…." (In re Fulton.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reference that lists alternatives but does not disparage or discourage particular alternatives cannot be relied upon as teaching away to avoid a rejection. Examiners and practitioners should look for explicit criticism, discrediting, or discouragement in the reference before treating it as teaching away; mere presentation of alternatives is neutral.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teaching away does not automatically defeat an anticipation or obviousness rejection—specific evidence required
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference's teaching away (e.g., showing an embodiment is less than optimal) does not vitiate the fact that it is disclosed and can still anticipate or render obvious the claimed invention (Celeritas; Merck; Gurley).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When an applicant argues that a reference teaches away, evaluate whether the reference contains explicit criticism/discouragement or whether there is additional discovery beyond the prior art. The mere showing that an embodiment is suboptimal or inferior does not remove it from consideration as prior art. Refer to MPEP §§2131.05 (anticipation) and 2145 (obviousness) for more detailed treatment of teaching away in each legal context.
